title: Week 8 · Nov 3 – Nov 10, 2026
sub: LIBERO moka pots: policy results, label strategy, and which π₀.₅ layers a value function needs
headline: Started from the Nov 3 mentor meeting: get the first policy results, test a second way of making advantage labels, and find which language-model layers carry progress without the flicker.

meeting.t: **Where we are (week 7):** the ResNet value function is the steadier progress tracker; π₀.₅ is more accurate, mainly by recognising hard vs easy scenes from the first frames, but flickers more.

The flicker has two separate sources: π₀.₅'s frozen language-model layers, and fine-tuning its vision encoder. A vision-encoder-only value function never beat the ResNet (frozen: steady but less accurate; fine-tuned: accurate but noisy).
SeeQ finds a VLM without pre-training performs on par with a ResNet for value learning. Given compute, hold off on pre-training for now and keep pushing with smaller models and limited data.

Advantage labels: training V on all 900 rollouts and labelling the same rollouts could be circular. Three valid options: (1) train on all, label all (simplest; risk of degenerate advantages if V memorises outcomes), (2) a new held-out rollout set (cleanest; 2× the data), (3) 5-fold out-of-fold labels (most principled; already running). Run (1) too, for comparison.
Subtask: a quick test reads which pot the robot is on with ~97% accuracy, so the signal is there. SeeQ's full method (a subtask-scoped Q-function, different policy extraction) is still worth trying.
New direction from SmolVLA / SmolVLM: SmolVLA throws away the top half of its language model and loses little on LIBERO. Apply the same idea to the value function: find which π₀.₅ layers it needs.

plan.t: **Policy results:** no gain, and worse than no fine-tune. Base π₀.₅ 56.4%; success-only 40.6%; advantage-tagged 40.9% (+ tag) / 43.0% (− tag), same 330 held-out trials. The tagged policy also ignores its tag. Next: a fine-tune recipe that does not hurt, then labels.
**Train-all / label-all labels:** paused; the out-of-fold labels are already running. Code is ready if we want the comparison later.
**π₀.₅ out-of-fold labels:** built from the 5 π₀.₅ folds. More accurate V, but worse labels than the ResNet's (within-scene AUC 0.68 vs 0.74), so no policy fine-tune on them.

**Verify episode length in environment steps:** done. Rollouts are ~20 s of simulated time (median success 404 steps at LIBERO's 20 Hz); the videos play at half speed, and our earlier "seconds" labels were 2× too long.
**Revisit the language-model layer ablation:** done on the 825-episode data. Steadiness is flat through layer 15 and drops at layers 17–18; accuracy is the same at every depth.
**Scene-calibration scatter:** done. All three backbones rank scenes equally well (r ≈ 0.66); π₀.₅ commits about 2× more to its call, which is where its accuracy edge comes from.

**Can a value function pick between π₀.₅'s own action candidates?** No: π₀.₅'s 8 samples end ~2 mm apart, and choosing the best one with the simulator itself gains nothing that survives a repeat (+0.006, 95% CI −0.028 to +0.042). Steering stopped at the pre-check.

directions.t: **Truncated π₀.₅ value function (SmolVLA idea):** first result (seed 0): reading only the first 4 of 18 layers is the steadiest π₀.₅ value function so far (0.180 vs 0.152) at a small accuracy cost (MAE 0.169 vs 0.160); 9 layers ≈ all 18. Needs 2 more seeds.

**Pre-robot vs robot weights:** done. The top layers were already noisy in PaliGemma before robot training; robot training made the lower and middle layers more accurate and steadier, and took away the top layers' response to pot placement.
**A small VLM as the value backbone:** SmolVLM-256M/500M, 64 image tokens per frame, the first half of its language model, fully fine-tuned on one GPU.

**SeeQ-style subtask value + steering:** the value of finishing the current pot, conditioned on the subtask and on a candidate action; used to choose the best of several π₀.₅ action candidates at each step instead of fine-tuning the policy. The two pre-checks are queued (see the plan).

results_note: Results from this week, newest first.

scene_calibration.title: Scene calibration: do the value functions know which scenes are hard?
scene_calibration.question: Week 7 found π₀.₅ is more accurate mainly because it recognises hard vs easy scenes from the first frames. Here each dot is one of the 10 validation scenes (12 rollouts each): its actual success rate against the value predicted in the first 2 s of its rollouts.
verdict: **All three rank the scenes about equally well:** correlation with the scene's success rate is 0.66 (ResNet), 0.68 (frozen π₀.₅), 0.65 (LoRA). Seed-to-seed spread is about ±0.06, so these are the same.

**The difference is how far they commit.** π₀.₅'s early values spread about twice as wide across scenes (slope against the true target 0.50–0.57 vs 0.23 for the ResNet). The ResNet hedges every scene toward the middle (−0.83 to −0.59, where the target runs −0.93 to −0.39).

That is where π₀.₅'s accuracy edge comes from: per-scene error 0.116–0.120 vs 0.150 for the ResNet. So the week 7 claim needs a correction: π₀.₅ is not better at *telling* hard scenes from easy ones; it is more willing to *say* so.

Why it matters for advantages: an advantage is a change in V within an episode, so a scene-wide offset cancels out. The ResNet's under-commitment at the start costs accuracy but not advantage quality, consistent with its advantage labels doing better within scenes.

Caveats: 10 scenes only, so each correlation is uncertain (95% range for r = 0.66 is roughly 0.05 to 0.91); the spread and per-scene error differences are the firmer result. LoRA is one seed. "First 2 s" = the first 40 environment steps at LIBERO's 20 Hz (see the episode-length card).
scene_calibration.source: val_predictions.parquet of runs 18237895–97 (ResNet), 18237898–900 (frozen π₀.₅), 18258391 (LoRA); frames with frame_index < 40; reports/site/content/scene_calibration.json

findings.title: Fine-tuning makes the policy worse: 56% before, ~41% after
findings.question: The fine-tuned policies scored ~41%. How does the original π₀.₅, without any fine-tuning, do on exactly the same 330 trials?
verdict: **Base π₀.₅: 186/330 = 56.4%.** Success-only fine-tune 40.6% (−15.8 points, 95% CI −22 to −9); tagged with the positive tag 40.8% (−15.5); negative tag 43.0% (−13.3).
The losses are largest on the easiest scenes (91% → 52%, 85% → 61%); two scenes improve (15% → 55%, 61% → 73%), so the fine-tune changes behaviour a lot, mostly for the worse.
Together with the tag check: the fine-tune costs ~15 points and the tag was never learned, so the advantage labels have not really been tested yet.
Next: find a fine-tune recipe that does not hurt (frozen vision encoder, lower learning rate, earlier checkpoints), then compare labels.

findings.title: The tagged policy ignores its tag
findings.question: The advantage-tagged policy scored the same with the positive and the negative tag. Does it react to the tag at all?
verdict: **Actions:** on 320 held-out frames, flipping the tag (same random noise) moves the action by **2%** of what the policy's own sampling noise does, and on no frame by more than the noise. That is even less than for the success-only policy, which never saw a tag (4%).
**Training data:** the policy predicts its own training actions exactly as well with the flipped tag as with the correct one (loss 0.00689 vs 0.00689).
So the policy never learned what "positive" and "negative" mean; the evaluation result says nothing yet about whether better labels would help.

Possible causes: the labels say too little about the actions (73% vs 66% positive in successes vs failures), or a word in the prompt read through a frozen language model is too weak a signal. Next: a fine-tune with an oracle tag (tag = rollout outcome) separates the two.

findings.title: Truncated π₀.₅ value function: fewer layers, less flicker (1 seed)
findings.question: SmolVLA drops the top half of its language model and loses little. Does a π₀.₅ value function that reads only the first 4 or 9 of the 18 language-model layers flicker less, and is it still as accurate?
verdict: **All 18 layers:** steadiness 0.152, MAE 0.160. **First 9:** 0.158, 0.162. **First 4:** **0.180**, 0.169 (seed 0, 120 held-out rollouts, same recipe).
Flicker falls with every cut (step-to-step noise 0.101 → 0.092 → 0.085), and accuracy drops only a little. Pot-on-stove response is similar (+0.03–0.04).

The 4-layer model is the steadiest π₀.₅ value function so far, but still below the ResNet (0.247), and one seed is not enough: the bar we set was clearly above the full model's 0.166 ± 0.025 (3 seeds).
Next: 2 more seeds of the 4- and 9-layer models.

findings.title: Per-layer probe: the flicker enters in the last 2–3 layers
findings.question: Same small value head on frozen features from each of π₀.₅'s 19 language-model layers (825 episodes, 3 seeds): where does steadiness drop, and does accuracy change with depth?
verdict: **Layers 0–15 are about equally steady** (0.14–0.16; layer 0 0.156 ± 0.019, layer 13 0.152 ± 0.006). It drops only at the top: layer 17 0.122, layer 18 **0.107**, final 0.116.
The response to the first pot landing on the stove disappears at the same depth (+0.05 at layers 0–15, ~0 at 17+).
**Accuracy barely changes with depth** (MAE 0.173–0.178, 0.184 at layer 18). Separating successes from failures is best in the middle (AUC 0.837 at layer 13 vs 0.797 at layer 0).

**The earlier probe's "steady fall from layer 1" was small-data noise.** Rerun on the same 375 fixed-layout episodes: layer 0 0.107 ± 0.023, layers 1–17 0.079–0.094 (the layer 0 → 1 drop is ~1 sd), final 0.055. On both sets the final layer is worst and the earlier layers are about equal; with more layout variety every layer is steadier and the drop sits clearly at the top.

findings.title: Before robot training: the top layers were already noisy
findings.question: Same per-layer probe on PaliGemma, the vision-language model π₀.₅ started from, before any robot training. Did robot training make the top layers noisy, or were they noisy already?
verdict: **PaliGemma:** steadiness drifts down with depth, 0.146 at layer 0 to 0.113 at layers 17–18. **π₀.₅:** flat around 0.15 through layer 15, then 0.12 / 0.11 at layers 17–18. Both end at about the same level.
**Robot training made every layer more useful:** accuracy MAE 0.195–0.207 → 0.173–0.184 and success-vs-failure AUC 0.66–0.73 → 0.79–0.84; middle layers got steadier (layer 11: 0.119 → 0.159).
**It also removed something at the top:** PaliGemma's top layers still respond when a pot lands on the stove (+0.05); π₀.₅'s do not (≈ 0 from layer 17).
So the top-layer noise is inherited, not caused by robot training, and cutting π₀.₅ before layer 17 keeps the layers robot training improved.

findings.title: First policy results: the advantage tag does nothing
findings.question: Does fine-tuning π₀.₅ with ResNet advantage tags (positive = this step made progress) beat fine-tuning on successes only?
verdict: **Success-only:** 134/330 = **0.406**. **Advantage-tagged, positive tag:** 135/330 = **0.409**. **Same policy, negative tag (control):** 142/330 = **0.430**. The untouched base π₀.₅ scores **0.564** on the same trials (next-but-one card).

All three are within noise of each other (±~0.05 at 330 trials). The negative tag should hurt if the policy used the tag; it does not, so either the policy ignores the tag or the labels carry little usable signal.
Setup: 33 rollouts on each of the 10 held-out scenes, environment seed 7, 5000 fine-tuning steps each, ResNet 5-fold out-of-fold labels (20-step lookahead, 70% positive).
Diagnosis (next cards): the tagged policy does not use its tag at all.

findings.title: π₀.₅ out-of-fold labels: a more accurate value, worse labels
findings.question: The ResNet labels gave no policy gain. Would labels from the more accurate π₀.₅ value function (same 5 folds, same rule) be better?
verdict: **Value accuracy:** π₀.₅ out-of-fold MAE 0.182 vs ResNet 0.195 (better).

**Labels:** within-scene AUC (does the share of positive steps separate successes from failures in the same scene?) **0.68** vs ResNet **0.74** (worse). Positive share inside successes vs failures: 72% vs 66% (ResNet 73% vs 66%). Near the end of failed rollouts 70% of steps are still positive (ResNet 64%).
The two label sets agree on 65% of steps (57% expected by chance); their advantages correlate at only 0.27.

Why: an advantage is a change in V over 20 steps, so V's flicker goes straight into the label. π₀.₅'s accuracy comes from judging scene difficulty early, which cancels out in a change; its extra flicker does not.
**Decision:** no policy fine-tune with π₀.₅ labels; both label sets are weak (only ~7 points between successes and failures), which fits the no-gain policy result.

findings.title: Steering pre-check: π₀.₅'s candidates are too alike to choose between
findings.question: SeeQ-style steering samples several action chunks and executes the one a value function likes best. Before training any Q-function: do π₀.₅'s candidates differ, and does choosing between them change success?
verdict: **Spread:** at 920 decision points in 10 rollouts, the 8 sampled chunks end a median **1.9 mm** apart, while the arm moves 22.7 mm per chunk. The gripper command differs between candidates at only 7% of decision points.

**Headroom:** at 4 points in each of 10 rollouts, each candidate was run to the end twice from the same exactly-restored simulator state. Picking the best candidate on the first run and scoring it on the second gives **+0.006** success (95% CI −0.028 to +0.042), i.e. nothing. The apparent +0.10 for the in-sample best is luck.
**Decision:** stop steering here. If the simulator itself cannot pick a better candidate, a learned Q cannot either. Widening the spread would mean changing the base policy's sampling.
Caveat: 10 states and 2 repeats per candidate.

findings.title: Episode length: rollouts are ~20 s of simulated time, not ~40 s
findings.question: The mentor noted that ~40 s seemed long for a LIBERO task. How long are the rollouts in environment steps and in seconds?
verdict: **Steps:** successful rollouts take 348–516 environment steps (median 404); failures hit LIBERO's 520-step limit for this suite. One recorded frame = one environment step.

**Seconds:** LIBERO's environment runs at **20 Hz** (`control_freq=20` in LIBERO's env wrapper; our rollout script keeps the default). So a median success is **~20 s** of simulated time (348–516 steps = 17–26 s), and the cap is 26 s.

**Why it looked like ~40 s:** the rollout videos are saved at 10 fps (`imageio.mimwrite(..., fps=10)` in `scripts/libero_rollouts.py`, copied from openpi's LIBERO example), so they play at half speed. Example: a 382-step success is a 38.2 s video but 19.1 s of robot time.

**What changes:** only time labels. Our scripts assumed 10 Hz, so every "seconds" number on the earlier pages is doubled: the "2 s" steadiness lag and advantage lookahead (20 steps) are really **1 s**, "AUC at 5 / 10 s" is at 2.5 / 5 s. The metrics themselves, the labels and the fine-tunes are unchanged, because everything is computed in steps.
Week 7 is kept as the pre-meeting snapshot with the old labels. From week 8 on, times are given in steps and real (20 Hz) seconds.
